newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Taleban concede lost ground but vow counterattack.
newsitem.headline: Taleban concede lost ground but vow counterattack.

text.p: Aghanistan's Taleban admitted for the first time on Monday it had lost key towns north of the capital to forces of former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood.

Travellers said that Masood forces continued to hold territory as far south as the town of Charikar, an hour's drive north of Kabul, but intermittent exchanges of gun- and rocket fire were heard around the town.
Journalists were not permitted to the areas to confirm the reports.
The country's purist Islamic government lost Charikar and the frontline town of Jabal os-Siraj in weekend fighting, its worst setback since taking the capital Kabul 17 days ago.

Acting Deputy Foreign Minister Sher Mohammad Stanakzai admitted suffering the losses but said the Taleban were successfully defending the key military airbase of Bagram and roads 30 minutes' drive north of Kabul.
"Jabal os-Siraj at the moment is with them, but Bagram airbase is with Taleban and even our forces are ahead of Bagram airbase as well," he told a news conference.
Independent sources confirmed the airbase appeared to remain in Taleban hands, but they said Taleban was not in complete control of the perimeter or of the road leading to the base.

In less than a week Masood, a formidable guerrilla fighter during the Soviet occupation of the 1980s, has emerged from his stronghold in the Panjsher valley 80 km (60 miles) north of Kabul to roll the Taleban back almost to the capital.

Kabul itself was quiet on Monday with Taleban fighters less visible than usual. Stanakzai said Masood did not have the strength to take the capital but said the Taleban was reinforcing its defences in case.
"I am quite sure they do not have the capability and the capacity to come back to Kabul. For the past two weeks they have been trying but still they have not been able.
"And we have already strengthened our positions in the frontline and also we have taken proper measures and precautions around Kabul," he said.
Stanakzai dismissed the reverses as temporary and said the Taleban would soon counter-attack and resume its assault on the Panjsher, its original target before the Masood offensive.

"Some of their elements have created problems at the backside, so now we have decided to clear our rear. After that we will go ahead and Panjsher valley will not be that difficult for us because now Masood is already finished," he said.

Afghan watchers doubted it would be so easy. They said that Masood appeared to have been successful in mobilising local commanders throughout the plains north of Kabul, inflicting heavy casualties on Taleban forces unused to such tactics.
The Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press (AIP) quoted witnesses in the eastern city of Jalalabad as saying on Monday that many Taleban casualties had been ferried there.
Stanakzai admitted the Taleban had suffered casualties but said he did not have figures.
He said some of the wounded were being transferred from Kabul to the southern city of Kandahar, partly to use better facilities and also to make room for more casualties.
"We do not have the same facilities here in Kabul especially in the military hospital," he said.

He also dismissed reports of an uprising in the western city of Herat, but said that pro-Masood elements in the country's western region appeared to be preparing to cause what he called provocations against the Taleban authorities there.

"Those people who had escaped to the Iran side, according to our reports, want to create some problems on the border, but we are fully aware of the situation and we have answered them in the past," he said.
